It's much less than that. For some background, read more on subsonic laminar flow across porous boundaries (such as https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0045793006000892). Basically, the flowing fluid encounters the obstacle and builds a small high pressure zone at that point. Past that point, a low pressure boundary develops along the obstacle and a laminar flow gradient is observed as distance from the obstacle increases. This is a fairly stable system and will remain as long as the fluid flow is in force. In plain English, it means that the air itself forms a significant barrier along the surface of the original barrier - five percent transition into the porous barrier would be a very generous estimate.

So yes, it does now go out left, right, up, and down; but it is going slower, and thus will not go as far.

Again, while your intermediate conclusion is correct, you seem to make a huge assumption that low velocity of aerosols limits their spread distance. This is a huge leap, and is completely incorrect. Aerosols are, by definition, a suspension of solid or liquid in a gas that will remain airborne for a long period of time. A vast majority of droplets produced by human respiratory action appear to be aerosols less than 10 um in diameter (ref https://www.liebertpub.com/doi/10.1089/jam.1997.10.105) and they quickly evaporated (on the order of 0.8-1.0 sec) so that their statistical mode was 1-2 um (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021850208002036?via%3Dihub).
